title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
City of Edmonton
Closing Date: October 19, 2026, 11:59 PM (MDT)
This is your chance to join Canada’s top public sector data science program!
Collaborating with teams across the Corporation, Senior Data Scientists bridge the divide between raw data and action, with an emphasis on solving real world problems and operationalizing solutions.
The Senior Data Scientist position is dedicated to leading and shaping end-to-end data science projects. This role serves as the driving force behind data science at the City of Edmonton and the application of insights to fulfill organizational objectives.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
What You Will Do

Project Intake: Decide on whether a project requires data science approaches such as machine learning, clustering, and forecasting. Do research on potential solutions, and project directions.
Project Leadership: Lead and manage complex data science projects, aligning them with corporate objectives and incorporating project planning, scheduling, resourcing, risk assessment, and cost/benefit analyses. Guide junior staff and mentor data science students on projects, and coordinate efforts between those involved.
Data Analysis: Analyze large and intricate datasets to extract meaningful insights that drive strategic decisions, considering the size, scope, duration, risk, and complexity of the projects.
Model Development: Develop and implement advanced predictive models and algorithms to address business challenges, leveraging specialized systems and technology (e.g., Unix, Docker, Databases, Scripting) for production-level implementation.
Operationalization: Work with Community partners to design a solution that can be used by front-line staff, and monitor usage as a key metric of project success.
Quality Assurance: Rigorously test and validate data-driven solutions to ensure accuracy, reliability, and alignment with the organization’s strategic direction.
Performance Monitoring: Continuously monitor the performance of deployed models, adapting and interpreting them as necessary to reduce uncertainty and increase the likelihood of success. Collaborate with the Data and Analytics Ethicist to examine ethical implications. This includes preparing progress reports and escalating project concerns to project governance.
Model Optimization: Iteratively improve machine learning models as needed to enhance predictive accuracy and relevance to business goals.
Stakeholder Communication: Effectively communicate complex findings and insights to non-technical Community Partners, including senior management, to influence the Corporation’s strategic direction.
Continual Learning: Stay up to date with new advancements in the field of data science broadly, with a specific emphasis on learning innovative techniques directly beneficial to the end-to-end implementation of data science projects at the City.
Perform other related duties.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
Qualifications

Graduate University Degree in applied statistics, mathematics, engineering, computer science, or a related field.
8 years experience with an emphasis on complex operationalized artificial intelligence projects.
Project Management Professional (PMP) Designation is required. Applicants who currently do not possess their PMP Designation may be considered and if successful, will be required to obtain it within the first 12 months of employment.

title: Senior Data Scientist
text:
Skills Required for Success

Proficient in multivariate regression/classification, time series models, cluster analysis, anomaly detection, optimization, neural network models, supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques.
Experience using state of the art machine-learning techniques (e.g., BERT, YOLO, XGBoost).
Proficiency in relational databases, SQL, and scripting languages (e.g., R, Python).
Experience with Generative AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks and architectures.
Experience with agent development frameworks such as Google ADK (or equivalents like LangGraph or LlamaIndex) and self-hosted model inference such as Ollama or vLLM.
Strong programming skills with experience in software development in a collaborative environment.
Demonstrated success in applying machine learning and statistical methods to solve practical problems.
Inherently motivated, intellectually curious, and inclined towards taking proactive actions.
Strong critical thinking, consensus-building, and influential skills.
Self-directed and capable of managing complex projects independently.
Proficient in project management with a track record of implementing improvements at organizational, departmental, and operational levels.
Effective communication skills tailored for diverse audiences, proven through successful information dissemination and active listening.
Alignment to our Cultural Commitments and Leadership Competencies.
Embracing a culture of equity, diversity, reconciliation and inclusion.
Applicants may be tested.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Research checked: October 8, 2026
Scope: Publicly available resources located online about the City of Edmonton’s Data Science and Research (DSR) team, publicly named members and collaborators, named projects, and the municipal context in which the team works. This is a source-based profile, not a complete staff directory or internal project register.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Overview
The City describes DSR as a team applying data science and artificial intelligence (AI) to operational municipal problems. Its public examples emphasize working with service-area staff and subject-matter experts, selecting methods that fit the decision, and planning for operational use rather than treating a model as a stand-alone research result. A 2025 presentation describes the group as a centralized team formed in 2020; a City article about WildEdmonton says it was founded in 2021. The sources may be describing different milestones, so the exact founding date is unclear.
The City article describes the team as having eight members at the time it was written, but it does not name them all. The 2025 Upper Bound session identifies four team presenters. Those four are the publicly named members that can be confidently associated with the team from the sources found here; this should not be read as a complete or current roster. A 2018 City data-science event identifies earlier contributors, shown separately below.
In September 2026, Taproot reported that the applied AI division had completed 77 projects and had 50 at different stages in its queue. Public coverage therefore documents only a fraction of the team’s work; the project list below is limited to initiatives for which a public source was found.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Publicly Documented Projects
Names, status, and level of attribution below follow the linked sources. “Current” indicates described as active or operational in the cited material, not independently verified as of the research date.



Project
Purpose and public status
People or partners linked in sources




Ember Wise / Amberwise
Wildfire-risk monitoring and forecasting. The Upper Bound presentation describes use of weather, forest-fuel, and topographic information; a location-based risk component is operational, while use of calls-for-service data to explore behavior-related ignition risk was still in development. Amii’s session description spells the name “Amberwise”; the presentation notes use “Ember Wise.”
Zehra Shah presented this work.


Residential safety-code inspection triage
A model to help prioritize discretionary residential safety-code inspections. The 2025 talk stresses that mandatory inspections remain required and describes choosing error thresholds with inspectors and operational partners. Earlier City and award coverage describes the Safety Codes Inspection Efficiencies (SCIE) initiative; public sources do not establish that every historical and current model version is identical.
Clayton Clemens presented the 2025 project. Ben Gready is associated with the earlier SCIE initiative.


Repair
A map-based workflow for filtering and prioritizing pothole reports, with historical information and next-week pothole estimates by road zone. The Upper Bound talk says the team moved from trying to predict individual notifications to forecasting counts by zone because report descriptions and images were often missing. A voice-activated reporting app was shown as a prototype.
Taher Abbasi presented the project.


WildEdmonton
City–University of Alberta wildlife monitoring partnership, running since 2018. The City’s account says the DSR team built an AI-assisted image workflow using Microsoft’s CameraTraps MegaDetector to identify and filter images containing people, improving privacy and processing efficiency for wildlife research.
City of Edmonton, University of Alberta, and DSR; the City identifies Clayton Clemens as a Senior Data Scientist involved in the work.


Unison
Public-safety data and deployment tool that combines partner incident-demand information into a shared operating picture. Reporting describes Decide for forecasting areas of demand and Track for monitoring trends and interventions. Its stated approach includes data minimization and excluding sensitive attributes and crime data that could produce feedback loops.
Kris Andreychuk is identified as an architect of the tool. Reporting names City and community partners.


Text Depot
Internal search and analysis tool for municipal text records. The City of Edmonton GitHub repository describes a dashboard for searching and analyzing text stored in Elasticsearch. An Apolitical case study attributes the broader platform to DSR and describes its internal use.
Attributed to the DSR team in the case study; the City maintains a public GitHub repository for the dashboard.


Exposure
Earlier project that scraped online “body rub” listings to help outreach workers identify people who might need assistance. Andreychuk said the project was taken over by police and later ended after the source site shut down.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; not a current DSR project.


Symbol Smart
Image-detection application intended to identify hate symbols. Andreychuk described the project as stalling because the departments that could use it could not agree on ownership.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting; status described as unsuccessful/stalled.


Used-needle collection route optimization
Route-optimization work for pickups from public bins. Andreychuk described learning that operational staff did not find the proposed routes useful; the public account does not document its eventual disposition.
Discussed by Kris Andreychuk in 2026 reporting.


Workforce-injury reduction
A project described as upcoming in September 2026 reporting; no public project name, technical details, or assigned team members were provided in the source.
No individuals identified in the source.



The City and partner sources also refer to broader AI and data-science work, but do not publish a complete list of the 77 reported completed projects or the 50 queued projects. The items above are the named initiatives substantiated in the sources collected here, not an exhaustive portfolio.

title: City Of Edmonton Data Science And Research Team
text:
Source Notes And Limitations

The 2025 Amii session names four presenters; the City-published WildEdmonton article says the team had eight members but does not name the other four. Neither source establishes the full present-day staffing roster.
Public accounts differ on whether the team was formed in 2020 or founded in 2021. Both claims are retained here rather than selecting one without evidence.
The wildfire project name appears as “Ember Wise” in the presentation materials and “Amberwise” in Amii’s session summary.
Project names, operating status, and member associations are limited to what the cited public sources state. Similar project labels do not by themselves prove that models described in different years are the same implementation.
Some project descriptions rely on reporting and partner case studies rather than a City project page. Links are included so readers can distinguish those accounts from City-published resources.
